name: How to tell whether search got better: silver labels from Google's weighted tags, hide-and-recover checks, and a person rating rendered result grids
what_it_is: A small test kit that fits a small budget of real searches. (1) A frozen request set of 25 requests (literal themes, plain moods, motion) with a silver answer set from Google's tag weights where the tag means what the request means. (2) Hide-and-recover: blank the tags of a seeded 20% of Google families (about 350, the size of the real gap), run the requests, and see whether those fonts still surface. (3) A noise floor: every request run twice per variant, self-overlap reported. (4) Blind side-by-side grids that the person rates, names hidden, one fixed sample text. (5) Later, free signals from real use (shortlist and cull actions) with interleaved results. Output: a per-variant table of silver precision, hidden-recovery ratio, self-overlap, A/B win rate with a sign-test result.
provider_and_url: Silver source: Google Fonts tags https://github.com/google/fonts/tree/main/tags (families.csv, 'human assessed'; quant.csv). Method sources: Carterette, Bennett, Chickering, Dumais, 'Here or There: Preference Judgments for Relevance', ECIR 2008, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/here-or-there-preference-judgments-for-relevance/ ; Thomas, Spielman, Craswell, Mitra, 'Large Language Models Can Accurately Predict Searcher Preferences', SIGIR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10621 ; Sakai, 'Laboratory Experiments in Information Retrieval: Sample Sizes, Effect Sizes, and Statistical Power', https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-981-13-1199-4 ; Radlinski, Kurup, Joachims, 'How Does Clickthrough Data Reflect Retrieval Quality?', CIKM 2008, https://www.cs.cornell.edu/people/tj/publications/radlinski_etal_08b.pdf ; Kitajima et al. 2024 (missing and noisy font tags), https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15236 ; 'Reading != Seeing: Diagnosing and Closing the Typography Gap in Vision-Language Models', https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08497 ; O'Donovan et al. 2014, https://www.dgp.toronto.edu/~donovan/font/fontSelection.pdf .
catalog_coverage: Counted by me. Silver labels exist for 1,611 of 1,760 Google families (1,523 with a flat Expressive vector, 88 with mood rows only at axis positions) and for none of the 339 non-Google families (Velvetyne 63, Collletttivo 26, Tunera 23, Use & Modify 163, Fontshare 64); 149 Google families have no mood row. So silver labels can score only the Google part of any result list; the libre-foundry picks (4-16 of 15-24 per search, mean 42%) can only be judged by the person. Usable silver sets (families with weight >= 60 among 1,611; in brackets the ones flagged 'very common', which the app's own prompt tells the model to avoid): Active 72 (3), Excited 108 (3), Loud 155 (24), Calm 247 (58), Futuristic 84 (8), Techno 46 (5), Sophisticated 38 (1), Fancy 57 (3), Playful 160 (2), Happy 90 (2), Childlike 59 (1), Cute 57 (0), Rugged 249 (20), Vintage 465 (16), Business 262 (46), Competent 167 (45), Awkward 249 (2), Wacky 43 (0), Stiff 88 (11), Innovative 41 (2), Artistic 156 (6), Sincere 243 (25), Pixel 43 (1), Brush 49 (2), Distressed 40 (0), Blackletter 16 (1), Handwritten 148 (5), Geometric 98 (25). 27 of 34 tags have at least 20 non-common positives, enough for a stable precision@20; Stencil 11, Medieval 11, Art Deco 7, Inline 8, Blobby 13 do not.
granularity: Per family (Google labels are per family). Grids can show one style per font; use the regular upright and one fixed sample text for every font.
signal_type: Semantic mood labels, human assessed by Google, used as a proxy answer key; plus the person's own visual judgement of rendered grids as the real answer key.
mood_dimensions_covered: Which requests silver labels can judge, by evidence. Tag-faithful (the tag means what a person would mean): Pixel, Brush, Blackletter, Distressed, Handwritten, Geometric, Loud, Playful, Cute, Childlike, Sophisticated, Fancy, Happy, Excited, Vintage, Calm. In my runs the model's Google picks hit the query's own tag for Pixel 20 of 20, Blackletter 14 of 19, Loud 10 of 20, Calm 5 of 19 (Haiku and Sonnet 5.5 pooled, tags visible; Calm is low because the prompt steers away from very common fonts, 58 of 247 Calm positives). Semantic mismatch (the tag exists but means something else): Active is lively script and comic display (top: Faster One 94, Aguafina Script 93, Story Script 91, Arizonia 90, Kaushan Script 89); corr(Active, Futuristic) = -0.01, corr(Active, Excited) = 0.44, corr(Active, Happy) = 0.37; Active >= 60 fonts have mean legacy slant 5.1 against 1.7 for the catalog. The model's 'fast movement' picks are wide racing and techno faces and hit Active >= 60 in only 0-4 of about 12 Google picks per run. Also Stiff, Awkward, Sincere, Innovative, Competent, Business. Motion/speed has no Google tag: build its silver set as a union (Active >= 60 or Excited >= 60: 152 families, 5 very common), plus shape traits once measured (legacy slant >= 4 or width >= 8 exist for only 706 families), and have the person check 40 of its members (about 4 minutes) before trusting it. Non-Google fonts: no silver at all.
query_style_specificity: Silver labels work for tight, tag-literal requests (pixel, blackletter, loud) and for the 'hide-and-recover' fairness check on any tag. They are close to useless as the sole judge for loose or abstract requests (calm, friendly) and for motion. The person's A/B votes are needed for those. Suggested mix of 25: 8 literal, 9 plain moods, 8 motion/action phrasings.
quality_evidence: Measured by me (scripts in docs/research/font-vibe-search/results/evidence/; Google tags snapshot from 2026-10-03; 54 real searches). Circularity: in the shipped prompt the model already sees the answer key. Share of silver positives (>= 60) whose tag is visible in the prompt line: Active 89%, Loud 93%, Excited 93%, Calm 100%, Futuristic 99%, Techno 100%, Playful 100%, Rugged 97%, Vintage 98%. So silver scoring of the current system measures reading, not seeing; it is valid only for (a) systems that do not read the tags, or (b) rows whose tags were hidden. Noise floor: identical prompt, 'fast movement or action': Haiku 4.5 pairwise overlap 0.19 (n=6; silver hits per run 2, 2, 3, 0, 4, 0, SD 1.6 on a mean of 1.8), Sonnet 5.5 low overlap 0.50 (n=5; hits 3, 2, 3, 3, 3). A single run per request cannot show differences smaller than that. Sensitivity checks that worked: hiding Google tags dropped Haiku's silver precision 57.5% -> 40% and halved its Google picks (clear, 17 points); changing Haiku to Sonnet moved precision 57.5% -> 68% (10 points, borderline at 4 requests); shuffling the Google block moved it 55% -> 54% (correctly no change). Statistics (computed by me, exact binomial and simulation): a two-sided sign test on A/B votes needs 18 wins of 24 (75%), 18 of 25 (72%), 21 of 30 (70%); its power at a true 70% win rate is 0.39 (n=24), 0.59 (n=30), 0.84 (n=60), at 75% it is 0.61 / 0.80 / 0.97. A paired t-test on per-request score differences (alpha 0.05) has power 0.65 at effect size d=0.5 and 0.81 at d=0.6 for n=24; 0.87 and 0.96 for n=40. With a per-request SD of 0.15 the 95% interval on a mean over 25 requests is about +-0.06. So 25 requests detect only clear improvements (about 10 points of precision, or 3 wins in 4). Literature: Carterette et al. (2008) report preference judgments ('A is better than B') are easier and steadier for assessors than absolute grades; Thomas et al. (2024): LLM labels were as accurate as third-party human labellers for web search relevance, but changed with simple paraphrases and need gold labels; a summary of Buckley and Voorhees puts 25 topics as the minimum for stable system comparison, and Sakai argues hundreds are needed for small effects [uncertain, secondary summaries]; a 2026 benchmark found vision-language models near chance on font style (best 33.6% vs 25% chance), so a vision model is not a trustworthy judge of rendered font grids [Claude not singled out in what I read]; O'Donovan et al. found MTurk raters' average majority vote was only about 74%, professional designers' font choices were preferred over MTurk choices only 53% of the time, and consistency among three professionals (Kendall tau 0.365) was no better than among MTurk workers (0.369), so a panel of strangers is noisy: use the one person whose taste the tool serves. [uncertain]
known_noise: Silver noise: label subjectivity (O'Donovan: pairwise agreement 69.6% average); missing labels are not negatives (Kitajima: very thick fonts are often not tagged heavy), so precision against silver understates true precision and recall against silver is unreliable; seasonal and odd tags (Kaushan Script Hanukkah 92); Exo 2, Saira, Teko have no Active tag anywhere. Google edits the tags (commits 2026-09-04 and 2026-09-23), so freeze a dated copy. Search noise: run-to-run overlap 0.19-0.50 (above). Test-prompt noise: my request-only prompts omit the wordmark; 1 of 24 Haiku runs refused and asked for it (0 of 24 Sonnet runs). Use the real request shape (wordmark, brief) in the harness.
name_and_memory_bias: Two directions. In the system: literal themes are found by name (72% of Pixel positives have a pixel-type word in the family name; Futuristic 14%, Techno 20%, Active 8%), so literal requests pass without testing anything. With Google tags hidden Haiku kept 40% silver precision and Sonnet 53%, so memory carries a lot. In the rating: the person must not see family names in the grids (O'Donovan removed font names from the interface to reduce familiarity bias and showed every font with the same word, 'handgloves'). Rate only on the letters.
untagged_rows: The hide-and-recover check is the test for this. Metric: for each request with silver set P, hide a seeded 20% fold of the Google families, then report hidden recovery ratio = (hidden positives in the top 20 / hidden positives) divided by (visible positives in the top 20 / visible positives); 1.0 means untagged rows are ranked fairly. I did not compute the ratio, but the crude proxy is stark: with all Google tags hidden Haiku returned 5.2 Google fonts per run instead of 12.2 for the motion request, and none (0 of 21 picks) for 'loud, shouting, impossible to ignore'; Sonnet 5.5 low was nearly unaffected (8.4 vs 9.0). Report the ratio per variant; a good fix moves Haiku's toward 1.
text_interference_risk: For rated grids yes: names bias taste, and different sample text changes the look. Render every font name-free in the same string, size, case and colour, the regular upright, shuffled position, left/right randomised. The outline's Stroop-effect point is unverified by me; O'Donovan's practice supports hiding names.
integration_path: A harness next to the app, not inside server/vibe.ts. eval/queries.json: [{"id":"q07","text":"pixel art, 8-bit video game","kind":"literal|mood|motion","silver":{"any":[{"tag":"/Theme/Pixel","min":60}],"exclude_common":true},"constraints":{"sources":[],"categories":[]}}] and a wordmark/brief block copied from a real project. eval/tags-2026-10-03.csv: frozen copy of Google's families.csv, flat rows, plus axis rows for the 88 axis-only families. eval/run.ts: for each variant (a named env: VIBE_MODEL, effort, order seed, tags hidden fold, labels on/off) and each query, call the same buildPrompt/askClaudeCode path twice and write eval/runs/<variant>/<qid>-<rep>.json {picks:[{family,reason}], usage, wall_ms}. eval/score.ts: per query and variant: silver precision@k and nDCG@k (gain = tag weight/100) on non-common Google picks; share of picks from indie rows; self-overlap between replicates; hidden recovery ratio; table to stdout. eval/grids.html (served by the app's existing card renderer): two result sets side by side for one request, blinded and randomised, three buttons (left better, tie, right better) and an optional 'clear miss' tick per grid, writing eval/votes.json; score.ts then prints win rate and the exact sign-test p. Live signal later: log each search's results and whether the person shortlists, culls or opens each font; compare two variants with team-draft interleaving (alternate picks from the two rankings) so one search tests both.
tokens_per_row: Not applicable to the harness. The hide-tags variants shrink the prompt (31.8k Haiku tokens instead of 57k), so they are cheaper per run; each variant is its own cache entry (1-hour lifetime measured), so run all of a variant's searches back to back.
vocabulary_alignment: Silver uses Google's tag names and weights directly. Requests must be mapped to tag expressions by hand (the 25-request file), once. Motion needs a union or trait rule because no Google tag means speed.
explainability: Per request the report lists silver positives, which the system hit, which it missed, and the person's vote and 'clear miss' ticks, so a changed score can be traced to named fonts.
determinism: The harness is deterministic except the model: replicate runs and report overlap, never a single run. Seeds fix the hidden fold, the shuffle and the request set.
build_effort: About a day for an agent: query file, runner, scorer with unit tests, the grid page and vote log; half a day more for the interleaving logger. 20 minutes of the person's time to approve the 25 requests and the silver rules.
per_search_cost_and_latency: Each real search takes about 8-18 s (Haiku mean 11.7 s, Sonnet 5.5 low 9.6 s, measured). The recommended run is 25 requests x 3 variants x 2 replicates = 150 searches, about 25 minutes sequential, plus 50 more for the hide-tags variant. API-equivalent cost at published prices is about $0.011 per cached Haiku search and $0.024 per Sonnet 5.5 search, so roughly $3-4 for the full run, nothing billed on the subscription (plan usage counts; limits not documented in what I read) [uncertain]. Run a variant's searches back to back inside the 1-hour cache lifetime. [uncertain]
one_off_cost: Scoring Google's tags is free (CSV already downloaded). The first full run is the 150-250 searches above.
human_effort: Write and approve 25 requests plus silver rules: about 20 minutes. Check the motion silver set: 40 fonts x 5 s about 4 minutes. A/B rating per round: 25 requests x 2 comparisons x 20-45 s = 17-38 minutes (my estimate, not measured on this person). Rating every font on a 0-3 scale instead (25 x 20 fonts x 3 systems x 3 s) would take about 75 minutes and is noisier; skip it. Re-rate 5 of the 25 a week later (about 3 minutes) to measure the person's own consistency [uncertain]. [uncertain]
asset_access: All inputs are already local: Google tags (scratch families.csv), the catalog, and the app's own font rendering. Do not re-fetch Google's CSV per run; freeze one copy.
licence_and_provenance: Silver data comes from Google's tag files (no licence text found in tags/; see indie-gap item) [uncertain]; used internally for scoring, not redistributed. Rendered grids use the catalog's fonts for the person's own review only. [uncertain]
etiquette: No external sites. Keep the claude -p runs sequential and capped (I ran 54 calls in 35 minutes without hitting a limit).
maintenance_and_freshness: Freeze the tag snapshot and the request file with a date; rerun on any change to prompt, model, catalog or tags. Google's tags drift (edited as recently as 2026-09-23), so compare variants only within one snapshot. Add 2-3 new requests per quarter and retire none, so older results stay comparable.
risks_and_limitations: 1) Silver labels read as ground truth when they are not (Active is not fast; 89-100% are visible in the prompt). Never report a silver score for a system that reads the tags without the hidden-fold version. 2) 25 requests give power only for large effects; most single-digit gains will be invisible. Do not ship on a 14-11 vote. 3) One rater's taste is the target, which is right for this tool but cannot be generalised. 4) The indie rows (about 40% of picks) have no silver at all, so a variant that only helps indie rows is visible only in the person's votes. 5) Run-to-run noise: report self-overlap and use replicates. 6) A vision LLM judge is not a substitute (font style accuracy near chance in the benchmark I read); a text LLM judge over tags is circular.
evaluation_hook: This item is the hook. First check, about 30 minutes: write the 25 requests, run the current system twice, produce the silver and overlap table, and rate one A/B pair of grids (current vs Sonnet 5.5 low) to confirm the page works.
recommendation_for_font_explorer: Use all of it, in this order, and keep it small. 1) Person-rated blind A/B grids are the primary measure for every decision; silver labels only for tag-literal requests and for fairness checks. 2) Freeze the Google tags and the 25 requests; run each variant twice and always report self-overlap (Haiku 0.19, Sonnet low 0.50 measured) next to any score. 3) Use hide-and-recover (seeded 20% fold, recovery ratio) as the test of any change to untagged rows; it detected a clear effect with about a dozen searches (Haiku 5.2 vs 12.2 Google picks per run). 4) Decide with the sign test: 18 of 24 wins or more, otherwise call it a tie and keep the cheaper variant. 5) Add shortlist/cull logging and interleaving later; it costs nothing per search but needs weeks of use. Smallest first step: write queries.json (25 lines) with the silver rule for 8 literal requests, run the current prompt twice for all 25, and print silver precision, indie share and self-overlap. That is 50 searches, about 9 minutes, about $0.60 API-equivalent. The evidence folder's scripts (eval_runs.py, eval2.py, pos_eval.py) already compute these quantities for the 'fast movement or action' request and four literal requests.
